claims.text: Computational design can identify lightweight HEA compositions with high energetic stability, low density, and high specific Young’s modulus.
The computationally designed lightweight HEAs may have low ductility.
The targeted computationally optimized lightweight HEAs have BCC or dual-phase structures.
Conventionally melted HEAs exhibit coarse dendritic grain structures.
The initial alloys exhibit a trade-off between high stiffness or strength and low ductility.
Controlled rolling followed by rapid annealing can refine the grain structure.
Advanced thermomechanical treatment will produce smaller grains and a more homogeneous microstructure in computationally optimized lightweight HEAs.
Grain refinement improves the balance between dislocation mobility and dislocation blockage.
The refined grain structure facilitates strain hardening and thereby improves ductility.
The refined grain structure maintains high stiffness and strength while ductility improves.
Greater microstructural homogeneity reduces stress-concentration sites and improves fracture resistance.

Combining computationally optimized lightweight compositions with advanced thermomechanical treatment will improve the overall combination of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
The treatment will increase ductility and fracture resistance while retaining yield strength and Young’s modulus comparable to or better than conventionally processed controls.
The approach is expected to work particularly for lightweight HEAs having high energetic stability.
The approach may not work for conventional equiatomic HEAs.
Excessive heat-treatment duration or temperature can cause grain growth that defeats the proposed refinement strategy.
Processing-induced undesired phase transformations may invalidate the proposed property improvements.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires only a measurable improvement and states that the quantitative gain is uncertain, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to exceed an illustrative 10% improvement as falsifying. A statistically significant improvement below 10% could therefore satisfy the stated prediction but fail the stated falsification criterion.
